reader.title: Lynching of L. M. Bell
bases: Three separately datelined dispatches (Hamburg, Pine Bluff, Shreveport) report that a mob took Bell from his home and hanged him to a tree over his wife's death (A1, A2, A4).

Bell was hanged by 'a mob' of 'indignant citizens' or 'villagers and neighboring farmers' with no legal process, as punishment for allegedly beating his wife to death (A1, A4, A8, A12). The size of the mob is never given, but every account describes a group.
Dispatches from Hamburg, Pine Bluff and Shreveport agree that Bell was hanged by a mob after his wife's death (A1, A2, A4).

summary.text: The lynching of L. M. Bell was the hanging of a planter by a mob near Hamburg, Arkansas, close to the Louisiana line, on the night of December 27, 1881.
Bell, called "Col." and "a prominent planter," was accused of beating his wife so badly that she died at Christmas.
Dispatches from three towns carried the story across the country, and at least one editor praised the lynching.
Bell lived near Hamburg, on or near the Arkansas-Louisiana line; one version of the Pine Bluff report put his home in Ashley County.
According to the Pine Bluff report, he "habitually abused his wife, an estimable woman and a Christian."
The Hamburg dispatch said he "whipped his wife so severely on Christmas that she died," while the Shreveport dispatch dated her death to Monday, December 26.
Her friends buried her, and her death so "excited the neighborhood," the Shreveport report said, that a mob formed on Tuesday night.
The mob took Bell from his home and hanged him to a tree, where his body was found early the next morning.

The Watertown Republican described the killers as "a mob of indignant citizens" who dragged him from his residence to "an adjacent tree," and the Staunton Vindicator said "the villagers and neighboring farmers" took him out on the night of the funeral.
The Hamburg dispatch placed the hanging twenty miles south of that town.
No report names any member of the mob or mentions an inquest, arrest or prosecution.
Three separate dispatches reached the wire on December 29: one datelined Hamburg, one from Pine Bluff and one from Shreveport.
The Shreveport version ran within two days in Nevada, California and Virginia papers, while the Pine Bluff version reached Mississippi, Missouri and Alabama weeklies in early January.
Bell's initials varied: most printings gave L. M., the Hamburg dispatch J. M., and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union's digest "Noll."
Headlines named the alleged crime rather than the mob: "Hanged for Whipping His Wife to Death," "Hung by a Mob for Abusing a Wife," and "A BRUTAL WIFE-MURDERER LYNCHED."
The wire copy praised the dead wife as "an intelligent and refined lady" and reported Bell's guilt with qualifiers such as "is said to have" and "it is alleged."
The Watertown Republican punned on his name with the headline "Bell-Hangers."
The Staunton Vindicator went further, calling it "the best use that lynch law has been put to for a long time" and quoting a maxim that a man who strikes a woman is a coward.
No report gave Bell's race or that of the mob.
The reports differ by a day on when the wife died, Christmas in the Hamburg and Pine Bluff versions and Monday, December 26, in the Shreveport version.

The Hamburg dispatch dated the hanging to December 28, but the Shreveport report's Tuesday-night mob and next-morning discovery suggest it took place on the night of the 27th, with the body found on the 28th.
The Gold Hill Daily News headed the Shreveport dispatch "Lynching in Louisiana," although its text placed Bell near Hamburg, Arkansas.

accounts.label: Hamburg dispatch
accounts.gist: Bell, a prominent citizen of the county, whipped his wife so severely on Christmas that she died; his neighbors hanged him twenty miles south of Hamburg on Dec. 28.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff dispatch
accounts.gist: A report reaching Pine Bluff said Bell, living on the state line about twenty miles from Hamburg (Ashley County in one version), had habitually abused his wife, who died on Christmas; the neighborhood was aroused and he was lynched.

accounts.label: Shreveport dispatch
accounts.gist: Bell's wife died Monday after his beating and was buried; a mob organized Tuesday night took him from his home and hanged him to a tree, where his body was found early the next morning.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Shreveport or Pine Bluff dispatch nearly verbatim under headlines naming Bell's alleged crime, 'A BRUTAL WIFE-MURDERER LYNCHED' and 'Hung by a Mob for Abusing a Wife.'
The Staunton Vindicator called it 'the best use that lynch law has been put to for a long time' and quoted a maxim against men who strike women.
The Watertown Republican's punning headline 'Bell-Hangers' called the mob 'indignant citizens'.

conflicts.note: A one-day difference; the Shreveport version adds that she was buried before the mob formed.

versions.value: Tuesday night (Dec. 27), body found the next morning

conflicts.note: The versions can be reconciled if the hanging took place on the night of Dec. 27 and the body was found on Dec. 28.
Most reports print L. M.; the Hamburg dispatch prints J. M.
Only the Weekly Clarion's reprint of the Pine Bluff item says twenty-eight; other printings of that item say twenty.
The Gold Hill headline 'Lynching in Louisiana' appears to follow the Shreveport dateline; its text places Bell near Hamburg, Arkansas.

record_check.dossier: Mob formed Tuesday night, Dec. 27; body found early Dec. 28 (the Hamburg dispatch says the hanging was on the 28th).
Near Hamburg, Ark. (about twenty miles south)
Col. L. M. Bell in most reports; J. M. only in the Hamburg dispatch
No report prints 'J. N.'; L. M. or J. M.
One person killed by the mob (Bell); his wife's earlier death is the alleged crime, not part of the mob's violence.
Not stated; described as 'Col.' and a 'prominent planter'.

info: Mob organized Tuesday night (Dec. 27, 1881); body found early the next morning (Dec. 28). The Hamburg dispatch dates the hanging 'yesterday' (Dec. 28).

Near Hamburg, Ark., near the Arkansas-Louisiana line; 'twenty miles south of' Hamburg (Hamburg dispatch), 'about twenty miles' (Pine Bluff dispatch), or 'twenty-eight miles' (one reprint); hanged to a tree near his residence.
Col. L. M. Bell (printed 'J. M. Bell' in the Hamburg dispatch and 'L. M. Noll' in one digest), described as a prominent planter or citizen; race not stated.
Accused of beating or whipping his wife so that she died; the Pine Bluff dispatch says he habitually abused her.
Unnamed; described as 'a mob', 'his neighbors', 'a mob of indignant citizens', and 'the villagers and neighboring farmers'.
